name: Copy
summary: Copies whatever you have selected (text, a file, an image) to the clipboard without removing it.
steps: Select the text or file you want.
Press the shortcut. Nothing visible happens, but it's now on your clipboard.
Paste it anywhere with Ctrl + V (⌘ + V on Mac).
tip: Copy works on files too. Select a file in File Explorer or Finder, copy it, then paste it into another folder to duplicate it.

name: Cut
summary: Removes the selected text and puts it on the clipboard, ready to paste somewhere else. It's the keyboard way to move things.
steps: Select the text you want to move.
Press the shortcut. The text disappears.
Click where it should go and paste.
tip: On Windows, Ctrl + X also moves files in File Explorer. On a Mac, Finder doesn't cut files: copy with ⌘ + C, then press ⌥ + ⌘ + V to move instead of copy.

name: Paste
summary: Drops whatever is on your clipboard at the cursor. The other half of copy and cut.
steps: Copy or cut something first.
Click where you want it.
Press the shortcut. You can paste the same thing as many times as you like.
tip: Pasted text bringing weird fonts and colors with it? Paste as plain text instead.

name: Undo
summary: Reverses your last action. Deleted a paragraph, moved the wrong file, or formatted the wrong cell? Undo it.
steps: Notice the mistake.
Press the shortcut once to step back one action.
Keep pressing to go back further.
tip: Undo works in File Explorer and Finder too. Accidentally dragged a folder somewhere? Undo moves it back.

name: Redo
summary: Brings back what you just undid. If you pressed undo one time too many, this is the fix.
steps: Undo something.
Press redo to bring it back.
Press again to step forward through each undo.
tip: Many Windows apps (Photoshop, VS Code, Figma) also accept Ctrl + Shift + Z, the same pattern as the Mac.

name: Select all
summary: Selects everything in the current box, document, folder or page in one press.
steps: Click inside the text box, document or folder first, so the shortcut knows what 'all' means.
Press the shortcut.
Now copy, delete or format everything at once.
tip: Select all, then hold Ctrl (⌘ on Mac) and click the few items you don't want to deselect them. It's faster than picking 40 files one by one.

name: Save
summary: Saves the file you're working on. Pressing it out of habit is the cheapest insurance against crashes.
steps: Press it whenever you pause.
The first time, a Save dialog asks for a name and folder.
After that it saves silently.
tip: Add Shift (Ctrl + Shift + S or ⌘ + ⇧ + S) for Save As in most apps, to save a copy under a new name.

name: Find on page or in a file
summary: Opens a search box that finds any word on the current web page, document, PDF or spreadsheet.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Type the word or phrase.
Press Enter to jump to the next match, Shift + Enter for the previous one.
tip: In File Explorer and Finder, the same shortcut jumps to the search box for files.

name: Print
summary: Opens the print dialog for the current page or document.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Pick a printer, or choose 'Save as PDF' / 'Microsoft Print to PDF'.
Press Enter to print.
tip: Need a PDF of a web page? Print it and choose Save as PDF. No extra software needed.

name: Clipboard history
summary: Shows the last things you copied, not just the latest, so you can paste any of them.
steps: Press Win + V. The first time, Windows asks to turn it on. Say yes.
Copy a few things as normal.
Press Win + V again and click any item to paste it.
tip: Pin the things you paste all the time (your address, an email signature) with the pin icon and they'll stay through restarts.
note: Mac has no built-in shortcut for this. Clipboard managers like Maccy add one.

name: Close a tab or window
summary: Closes the current browser tab, document or window without hunting for the tiny X.
steps: Make sure the tab or window you want to close is in front.
Press the shortcut.
Keep pressing to close tabs one after another.
tip: Closed one too many? Ctrl + Shift + T (⌘ + ⇧ + T) brings the last tab back.

name: Close or quit an app
summary: Closes the whole app, not just one window. On a Mac, closing the last window often leaves the app running; ⌘ + Q really quits it.
steps: Click the app you want to close.
Press the shortcut.
If you have unsaved work, the app asks first.
tip: On Windows, pressing Alt + F4 on the empty desktop opens the Shut Down menu.

name: Jump one word at a time
summary: Moves the cursor a whole word left or right instead of one letter at a time.
steps: Click in any text.
Hold Ctrl (Option on Mac) and tap the arrow keys.
The cursor hops word by word.
tip: Combine it with Backspace or Delete to fix a typo three words back without touching the mouse.

name: Select one word at a time
summary: Selects text a word at a time, which is much more accurate than dragging the mouse.
steps: Put the cursor at the start of what you want.
Hold Ctrl + Shift (Option + Shift on Mac).
Tap the arrow keys to grow the selection word by word.
tip: Overshot? Keep holding the keys and tap the opposite arrow to shrink the selection.

name: Delete a whole word
summary: Deletes the entire word behind the cursor in one press instead of letter by letter.
steps: Type a word you want to take back.
Press the shortcut once per word.
Keep going to delete several words.
tip: Ctrl + Delete on Windows (fn + ⌥ + Delete on Mac) deletes the word in front of the cursor instead.

name: Jump to the start or end of a line
summary: Sends the cursor to the very beginning or end of the current line.
steps: Click anywhere in a line of text.
Press Home (⌘ + ← on Mac) to go to the start, End (⌘ + → on Mac) for the end.
Add Shift to select up to that point.
tip: No Home and End keys on your laptop or 60% keyboard? They're usually Fn + ← and Fn + →.

name: Jump to the top or bottom of a document
summary: Jumps straight to the first or last line of a document, a long page or a spreadsheet.
steps: Click in the document.
Press the shortcut for the top or bottom.
Add Shift to select everything between the cursor and that point.
tip: In Excel, Ctrl + Home goes to cell A1 and Ctrl + End goes to the last cell with data.

name: Select text with the keyboard
summary: Holding Shift while you move the cursor selects everything it passes over.
steps: Put the cursor where the selection should start.
Hold Shift.
Use the arrows to grow the selection a letter or line at a time.
tip: Shift works with every movement shortcut: Shift + End selects to the end of the line, Shift + Ctrl + End to the end of the document.

name: Paste as plain text
summary: Pastes just the words, without the fonts, colors and links from wherever you copied them.
steps: Copy text from a website or email.
Click into your document or message.
Press the shortcut to paste it in the surrounding style.
tip: Works in Chrome, Edge, Google Docs, Slack, Teams and most modern apps.
note: In Microsoft Word, Ctrl + Shift + V pastes formatting instead. Use Paste Options > Keep Text Only there.

name: Open the emoji and symbol picker
summary: Opens a panel of emoji, symbols (©, °, →) and kaomoji you can insert anywhere you type.
steps: Click where you're typing.
Press the shortcut.
Type to search, for example 'thumbs', then press Enter.
tip: On newer Macs, the 🌐 / fn key on its own can open the emoji picker too (set it in Keyboard settings).

name: Delete to the start of the line
summary: On a Mac, deletes everything from the cursor back to the start of the line in one press.
steps: Put the cursor at the end of what you want gone.
Press ⌘ + Delete.
Everything to the left on that line disappears.
tip: On Windows you can do the same in two steps: Shift + Home to select to the start of the line, then Backspace.
note: Careful in Finder: ⌘ + Delete there moves the selected file to the Trash.

name: Switch between apps
summary: Flips between open apps without reaching for the taskbar or Dock.
steps: Hold Alt (⌘ on Mac).
Tap Tab to move through the open apps.
Let go to switch to the highlighted one.
tip: A single quick tap flips between your two most recent apps, which is perfect for copying between two windows.

name: See every open window (Task View / Mission Control)
summary: Zooms out to show every open window at once, plus your virtual desktops.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Click (or arrow to) the window you want.
Press Esc to go back without switching.
tip: Task View and Mission Control are also where you drag windows between desktops.

name: Show the desktop
summary: Minimizes everything so you can see the desktop. Press it again and every window comes back.
steps: Press Win + D.
Grab the file or shortcut from the desktop.
Press Win + D again to restore your windows.
tip: The 'boss key': one press hides everything on screen.
note: On a Mac, use the Show Desktop gesture (thumb and three fingers spread) or set a hot corner.

name: Snap a window left or right
summary: Snaps the current window to fill exactly half the screen, so two apps sit side by side.
steps: Click the first window and press Win + ←.
Windows offers your other apps for the right half. Pick one.
Press Win + → / ← again to move a window between halves and monitors.
tip: Add Win + ↑ or Win + ↓ after snapping to make quarter-screen windows.
note: Recent macOS versions can tile windows with the 🌐 fn + Control + arrow shortcuts. Older Macs need an app like Rectangle.

name: Maximize a window
summary: Makes the current window fill the screen, without going into full-screen mode.
steps: Click the window.
Press Win + ↑.
Press Win + ↓ to restore it to its old size.
tip: Win + Shift + ↑ stretches a window to the full height of the screen while keeping its width.
note: On a Mac, double-clicking a window's title bar zooms it to fill the screen.

name: Minimize or hide a window
summary: Sends the current window down to the taskbar or Dock.
steps: Click the window.
Press the shortcut.
Bring it back from the taskbar, Dock, or with Alt + Tab / ⌘ + Tab.
tip: On Windows, if the window is maximized, the first Win + ↓ restores it and the second minimizes it.

name: Hide an app
summary: On a Mac, hides every window of the current app instantly. It keeps running; it's just out of sight.
steps: Click the app.
Press ⌘ + H.
Switch back to it with ⌘ + Tab and its windows return.
tip: ⌥ + ⌘ + H hides every app except the one you're using. Instant focus mode.

name: Open Snap Layouts
summary: Shows a menu of window layouts (halves, thirds, quarters) for the current window. Windows 11 only.
steps: Click the window you want to place.
Press Win + Z.
Press the number of the layout, then the number of the zone (or just click it).
tip: Hover over a window's maximize button with the mouse to get the same menu.

name: Switch between windows of the same app
summary: On a Mac, cycles through the windows of the app you're in, for example between two Chrome windows.
steps: Open two windows of the same app.
Press ⌘ + ` (the key above Tab).
Each press moves to the next window.
tip: ⌘ + Tab switches apps; ⌘ + ` switches windows inside an app. Learn both and you'll rarely click a window again.
note: On Windows, hold Ctrl while clicking an app's taskbar icon to cycle through its windows.

name: Go full screen
summary: Puts the current app in full-screen mode, hiding the taskbar, toolbars and everything else.
steps: Click the app.
Press the shortcut.
Press it again (or Esc on Windows) to leave full screen.
tip: Great for reading, presentations and focus. In browsers it hides the tabs and address bar too.
note: F11 works in browsers and File Explorer on Windows; not every app supports it. On some laptops, press Fn + F11.

name: Create a new virtual desktop
summary: Adds a fresh, empty desktop, like a second monitor you can't see. Great for keeping work and personal apps apart.
steps: Press Win + Ctrl + D.
Open the apps you want on this desktop.
Close a desktop with Win + Ctrl + F4. Its windows move to the next desktop.
tip: Right-click a desktop in Task View (Win + Tab) to rename it, for example 'Work' and 'School'.
note: On a Mac, add a Space from Mission Control (⌃ + ↑), then click + at the top right.

name: Switch virtual desktops or Spaces
summary: Slides between your virtual desktops (Windows) or Spaces (Mac).
steps: Create at least two desktops.
Press the shortcut with ← or →.
Each desktop keeps its own set of windows.
tip: A full-screen app on a Mac gets its own Space, so ⌃ + ← / → also flips in and out of full-screen apps.

name: Screenshot part of the screen
summary: Lets you drag a box around anything on screen and capture just that part.
steps: Press the shortcut. The screen dims.
Drag a box around what you want.
Windows copies it to the clipboard (click the pop-up to mark it up); a Mac saves it to the desktop.
tip: On a Mac, add Control (⌃ + ⌘ + ⇧ + 4) to copy the screenshot to the clipboard instead of saving a file.

name: Screenshot the whole screen
summary: Captures the entire screen and saves it as an image file straight away.
steps: Press the shortcut. The screen flashes briefly.
On Windows, find it in Pictures > Screenshots.
On a Mac, it lands on your desktop.
tip: No PrtScn key? On many laptops it's Fn + PrtScn, or Win + Fn + PrtScn.

name: Screenshot one window
summary: Captures just the active window with no desktop clutter around it.
steps: Click the window you want.
Windows: press Alt + PrtScn to copy it. Mac: press ⌘ + ⇧ + 4, then Space, then click the window.
Paste it (Windows) or find it on your desktop (Mac).
tip: Mac window screenshots include a soft shadow. Hold Option while clicking to leave it out.

name: Open the screenshot and screen-recording toolbar
summary: On a Mac, opens a toolbar with every capture option, including screen recording, timers and where to save.
steps: Press ⌘ + ⇧ + 5.
Pick screen, window, area, or one of the record options.
Use Options to change the save folder or set a 5-second timer.
tip: Change the save location once here (for example to a Screenshots folder) and your desktop stays clean.
note: On Windows 11, open the Snipping Tool (Win + Shift + S, then the video icon) to record your screen.

name: Copy a screenshot instead of saving it
summary: On a Mac, add Control to any screenshot shortcut and it goes to the clipboard instead of becoming a file on your desktop.
steps: Press ⌃ + ⌘ + ⇧ + 4 and drag a box (or ⌃ + ⌘ + ⇧ + 3 for the full screen).
Nothing is saved to the desktop.
Paste it straight into an email, chat or document with ⌘ + V.
tip: Perfect for sharing quick screenshots in Slack or Messages without cluttering your desktop.
note: Windows' Win + Shift + S already copies to the clipboard by default.

name: Search for any app or file (Spotlight / Start)
summary: Opens system search so you can launch any app, file or setting by typing a few letters.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Type the first few letters of what you want, like 'calc'.
Press Enter to open it.
tip: This is the 'launcher' trick from the Top 10 video: it's faster than any Start menu or Dock you could organize.
note: On Windows you can also press Win + S to open search directly.

name: Open File Explorer or Finder
summary: Opens a new window for browsing your files.
steps: Press the shortcut.
A new File Explorer (or Finder) window opens.
Start typing a folder name to jump to it.
tip: Set File Explorer to open on 'This PC' or a favorite folder instead of Home in its Folder Options.

name: Open Windows Settings
summary: Opens the Settings app directly.
steps: Press Win + I.
Type in the search box at the top to find any setting.
Press Enter.
tip: Searching in Settings is much faster than clicking through menus. Try 'display', 'bluetooth' or 'default apps'.
note: On a Mac, open System Settings from the  menu or Spotlight. For the current app's settings, press ⌘ + ,.

name: Open the current app's settings
summary: On a Mac, opens Settings (Preferences) for whatever app you're using.
steps: Click the app.
Press ⌘ + , (comma).
Its settings window opens.
tip: Lots of Windows apps borrow this one too: Ctrl + , opens settings in VS Code, Slack, Discord and Teams.

name: Lock your computer
summary: Locks the screen instantly. Your apps stay open, but no one can get in without your password.
steps: Press the shortcut whenever you step away.
The lock screen appears.
Sign back in to pick up where you left off.
tip: In an office (and in IT), locking every time you stand up is the single best security habit you can build.

name: Open the Power User menu
summary: Opens a hidden menu with Device Manager, Disk Management, Terminal, Task Manager, Settings and shut down options.
steps: Press Win + X.
Each item has an underlined letter.
Press that letter (for example M for Device Manager) to open it.
tip: IT techs live in this menu. Win + X, then U, then U shuts the PC down without the mouse.

name: Open the Run box
summary: Opens Run, a tiny box that launches programs and folders by name.
steps: Press Win + R.
Type a command, for example 'notepad', 'cmd', or '%temp%'.
Press Enter.
tip: Useful ones: 'control' (Control Panel), 'appwiz.cpl' (uninstall programs), 'msconfig' and 'shell:startup'.

name: Open Task Manager or Force Quit a frozen app
summary: Opens Task Manager on Windows or the Force Quit window on a Mac, so you can close an app that has frozen.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Select the frozen app.
Click End task (Windows) or Force Quit (Mac).
tip: Task Manager also shows what's slowing your PC down. Sort by CPU or Memory to find the culprit.

name: Open Quick Settings
summary: Opens the Quick Settings panel with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, volume, brightness and Focus.
steps: Press Win + A.
Use the arrow keys and Space to toggle a setting.
Press Esc to close.
tip: On Windows 10, Win + A opens the Action Center, which has the same quick toggles at the bottom.
note: On a Mac, Control Center lives in the menu bar; there's no default shortcut for it.

name: Show or hide the Dock
summary: On a Mac, turns Dock auto-hide on or off, so you get the full height of your screen back.
steps: Press ⌥ + ⌘ + D.
The Dock slides away.
Move the pointer to the bottom of the screen to bring it back, or press the shortcut again.
tip: Great on small laptop screens: you get more room for every app.
note: On Windows, turn on 'Automatically hide the taskbar' in Settings > Personalization > Taskbar.

name: Open a new tab
summary: Opens a new browser tab with the cursor already in the address bar.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Start typing a website or search.
Press Enter.
tip: Ctrl + N (⌘ + N) opens a whole new window instead.

name: Reopen a closed tab
summary: Brings back the tab you just closed, with its history. Press it again to keep going back.
steps: Close a tab by accident.
Press the shortcut.
It reopens exactly where you left it.
tip: Closed the whole browser? Pressing it in a new window often restores every tab from the last session.

name: Switch to the next tab
summary: Moves one tab to the right. Add Shift to move one tab to the left.
steps: Open a few tabs.
Press the shortcut to step through them.
Add Shift to go backwards.
tip: On a Mac, ⌘ + ⌥ + → and ← also switch tabs in most browsers.

name: Jump to a specific tab
summary: Jumps straight to tab 1 through 8. The number is the tab's position from the left.
steps: Count where the tab is.
Press the shortcut with that number.
Ctrl + 9 (⌘ + 9) always jumps to the last tab.
tip: Keep your email or calendar pinned as the first tab, and Ctrl + 1 always takes you there.

name: Jump to the address bar
summary: Selects the address bar so you can type a new web address or search right away.
steps: Press the shortcut. The current address is highlighted.
Type over it.
Press Enter.
tip: Alt + D and F6 do the same on Windows. Ctrl + L also works in File Explorer's address bar.

name: Open a private (incognito) window
summary: Opens a private window that doesn't save history, cookies or what you type in forms after you close it.
steps: Press the shortcut in Chrome or Edge (InPrivate).
Browse as normal.
Close the window and the session is gone.
tip: Handy for logging into a second account or checking how a site looks when you're signed out.
note: In Firefox it's Ctrl + Shift + P (⌘ + ⇧ + P). Private browsing doesn't hide you from your employer or internet provider.

name: Bookmark the page
summary: Saves the current page to your bookmarks.
steps: Press the shortcut.
Pick a folder, or rename it.
Press Enter to save.
tip: Ctrl + Shift + B (⌘ + ⇧ + B) shows or hides the bookmarks bar.

name: Zoom in and out
summary: Makes everything on the page bigger or smaller. Works in browsers and most apps.
steps: Press the shortcut with + to zoom in.
Press it with − to zoom out.
Reset with Ctrl + 0 (⌘ + 0).
tip: Hold Ctrl and scroll the mouse wheel for smooth zooming, or pinch on a trackpad.

name: Reset zoom
summary: Puts the page back to 100% zoom.
steps: Notice that a page looks too big or too small.
Press the shortcut (that's a zero).
It snaps back to normal size.
tip: Browsers remember zoom per website, so if one site always looks huge, this fixes it for good.

name: Reload the page
summary: Refreshes the current page.
steps: Press the shortcut.
The page loads again.
Still broken? Add Shift for a hard reload that skips the cache.
tip: F5 also reloads on Windows. Ctrl + Shift + R (⌘ + ⇧ + R) is the hard reload that fixes most 'it looks wrong' problems.

name: Rename a file
summary: Starts renaming the selected file or folder without right-clicking.
steps: Click the file once to select it.
Press the shortcut. The name is highlighted (without the extension).
Type the new name and press Enter.
tip: In File Explorer, press Tab while renaming to jump to the next file and keep going. Select several files and press F2 to rename them all as a numbered series.

name: Create a new folder
summary: Creates a new folder in the current location, ready to be named.
steps: Open the location in File Explorer or Finder.
Press the shortcut.
Type a name and press Enter.
tip: On a Mac, select some files and press ⌃ + ⌘ + N to create a new folder with those files already inside.

name: Go up one folder
summary: Jumps to the parent folder, the one that contains the folder you're in.
steps: Open any folder.
Press the shortcut.
Keep pressing to climb toward the top of the drive.
tip: Alt + ← and → (⌘ + [ and ] on Mac) go back and forward through folders, like a browser.

name: See file properties (Get Info)
summary: Opens the details for the selected file: size, location, dates, permissions and more.
steps: Select a file or folder.
Press the shortcut.
Check its size, location or sharing settings.
tip: Select several files first and Windows adds up their total size.

name: Copy a file's full path
summary: Copies the selected file's full location (like C:\Users\you\file.pdf) to paste into a chat, script or upload box.
steps: Select the file.
Press the shortcut.
Paste the path wherever you need it.
tip: Pasting a full path into an 'Open file' box takes you straight to the file.
note: Ctrl + Shift + C is a Windows 11 File Explorer shortcut. On Windows 10, hold Shift, right-click the file and choose 'Copy as path'.

name: Delete a file (move to the Recycle Bin or Trash)
summary: Moves the selected files to the Recycle Bin or Trash, where you can still get them back.
steps: Select the files.
Press the shortcut.
Changed your mind? Undo (Ctrl + Z / ⌘ + Z) puts them back.
tip: Undo works right after deleting, so a slip of the finger is easy to fix.

name: Delete a file forever
summary: Deletes the selected files permanently, skipping the Recycle Bin or Trash.
steps: Select the files you're sure about.
Press the shortcut.
Confirm. They're gone for good.
tip: Use this for huge files you'll never need again, so they don't sit in the Recycle Bin taking up space.
note: There's no undo. Double-check what's selected first.

name: Preview a file instantly (Quick Look)
summary: On a Mac, shows a full preview of the selected file (PDFs, photos, videos, documents) without opening any app.
steps: Select a file in Finder.
Press Space.
Use the arrow keys to preview the next file. Press Space again to close.
tip: Hold Option and press Space to open the preview full screen.
note: Windows has no built-in equivalent. The free Microsoft PowerToys 'Peek' tool adds one (Ctrl + Space).

name: Show hidden files
summary: On a Mac, shows or hides the hidden files and folders in Finder.
steps: Open a folder in Finder.
Press ⌘ + ⇧ + . (period).
Hidden items appear faded. Press it again to hide them.
tip: Hidden files are usually hidden for a reason. Look, but don't delete them unless you know what they do.
note: On Windows, turn on View > Show > Hidden items in File Explorer.

name: Go to a folder by typing its path
summary: Lets you type or paste a folder path and jump straight there.
steps: Open File Explorer or Finder.
Press the shortcut.
Type or paste a path, for example ~/Downloads or C:\Users, and press Enter.
tip: On a Mac, ⌘ + ⇧ + G is the only easy way into hidden folders like ~/Library.
note: On Windows, this selects File Explorer's address bar (Alt + D does the same).
